name: Surveyor 5
intro: Surveyor 5 nearly didn’t make it: a leak on the way to the Moon forced engineers to invent a new landing plan in a hurry. It touched down on a steep slope inside a small crater in the Sea of Tranquility and became the first spacecraft to test what Moon soil is made of.
whyLeft: It was never designed to come home, and after working through several freezing lunar nights its power finally gave out in December 1967.
repurpose: It sits only about 25 km from Apollo 11, so a future rover visiting Tranquility Base could swing by and check how its parts aged.
funFact: Surveyor 5 is only about 25 km from where Apollo 11 landed less than two years later.

hotspots.title: Leaky engines
hotspots.text: After a course correction, helium gas that pushes fuel to these engines started leaking away. Engineers fired the engines early and lit the big braking rocket much lower than planned, only 1.3 km up. The rescue worked perfectly.

photo.alt: A Surveyor vernier rocket engine on a test stand
photo.caption: One of Surveyor’s small vernier engines, photographed on Earth for the Surveyor 5 mission report.

hotspots.title: Soil chemistry lab
hotspots.text: This box was lowered on a cord onto the ground to find out what the soil is made of. It discovered the Sea of Tranquility is like basalt, a dark volcanic rock found on Earth. That was the first chemistry test ever done on another world.

photo.alt: The bottom of the alpha-scattering instrument sensor head
photo.caption: The bottom of the chemistry instrument’s sensor head, photographed on Earth before flight.

hotspots.title: Magnet on the foot
hotspots.text: A small magnet on one footpad picked up bits of the soil. The amount stuck to it showed the dust holds a little bit of magnetic, iron-rich mineral.

hotspots.title: Engine blast test
hotspots.text: Two days after landing, engineers fired the engines for just over half a second while Surveyor sat on the ground. It disturbed only a little soil, useful news for Apollo planners worried about landing-engine blasts.

hotspots.title: Solar panel
hotspots.text: Surveyor 5 was tougher than expected. It slept through its first lunar night and woke up again, then kept working on and off until its last radio message on 17 December 1967.

hotspots.title: Hole-in-one
hotspots.text: From orbit, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter shows Surveyor 5 sitting inside a crater about 10 m wide, like a golf ball in a hole.

photo.alt: Surveyor 5 seen from orbit inside a small crater
photo.caption: Surveyor 5 inside its small crater, photographed from orbit by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.
